questions.q: Which water body forms India's natural boundary on the east, according to the chapter?
questions.a: The Bay of Bengal forms India's natural boundary to the east.

questions.q: In 1984 Prime Minister Indira Gandhi asked Rakesh Sharma, the first Indian astronaut to go into space, 'How does India look from space?' He replied, 'Saare jahan se achchha.' What did his reply mean?
o: India looked better than the whole world
India looked smaller than its neighbours
India could not be seen clearly from space
India looked like one great desert
questions.a: His reply meant that India looked better than the whole world.

questions.q: A ship starts off the west coast of India, sails round the southern tip of the country and then north towards the Ganga delta. Using the natural boundaries the chapter gives for the west, the south and the east, in which order does the ship pass India's sea boundaries?
o: Arabian Sea, then Indian Ocean, then Bay of Bengal
Bay of Bengal, then Indian Ocean, then Arabian Sea
Arabian Sea, then Bay of Bengal, then Indian Ocean
Indian Ocean, then Arabian Sea, then Bay of Bengal
questions.a: The Arabian Sea (west), then the Indian Ocean (south), then the Bay of Bengal (east).

questions.q:
Read the statements about the way the chapter describes India.
I. The islands are one of the five regions the chapter uses to describe India.
II. The Bay of Bengal forms a natural boundary of India in the east.
III. The great mountain zone is one of the five regions.
Which of these statements is/are correct?
questions.a: All three statements are correct.

questions.q:
Assertion (A): India's geographical features create a separation between India and the rest of the continent of Asia.
Reason (R): The Himalayas in the north, the Thar Desert and the Arabian Sea in the west, the Indian Ocean in the south and the Bay of Bengal in the east form natural boundaries around India.
Choose the correct option.
o: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true, but R is false.
A is false, but R is true.
questions.a: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A: these natural boundaries are what separate India from the rest of the continent.

questions.q: True or False? 'India gives its name to the subcontinent it is a part of.' Give the verdict and the reason.
questions.a: True. The region formed by India and its neighbours Pakistan, Bangladesh, Nepal, Bhutan, Sri Lanka and Myanmar is called the Indian Subcontinent, named after India.
s: States the verdict: True
Explains that the region of India and its six neighbours is called the Indian Subcontinent

questions.q: (a) Name the two natural features that mark India's western limits. (b) According to the chapter, which three things about India have its natural boundaries played a crucial role in shaping?
questions.a: (a) The Thar Desert and the Arabian Sea. (b) India's climate, culture and history.
s: (a) Names the Thar Desert and the Arabian Sea
(b) Names climate, culture and history

questions.q: Kiran says, 'The Indian Subcontinent is called a subcontinent because it lies to the south of Asia and is not a part of that continent.' Is she right? Give a verdict and support it with two facts from the chapter.
questions.a: No. (1) The chapter says India is a part of Asia, and the region is called a subcontinent precisely because it is part of the continent of Asia, not outside it. (2) The Indian Subcontinent is the region India forms together with its neighbours Pakistan, Bangladesh, Nepal, Bhutan, Sri Lanka and Myanmar, so it is a region within Asia.
s: Verdict: No, the subcontinent is part of Asia
States the chapter's reason for the name: it is called a subcontinent since it is part of the continent of Asia
States that the subcontinent is the region India forms with its neighbours, naming at least three of Pakistan, Bangladesh, Nepal, Bhutan, Sri Lanka and Myanmar

questions.q:
Class 7 of a school in Bhopal is making a wall chart called 'Flying over India'. Their teacher gives them this note: 'Our country is one of the largest in the world. A great mountain wall about 2500 km long runs along its north. Desert and sea mark its west, an ocean its south and a bay its east. To keep things simple we describe the country in five regions, one panel for each.'
(a) What is India's rank among the countries of the world by size?
(b) Name the mountain wall in the north.
(c) Name the five regions the class will draw.
(d) A classmate wants a sixth panel for Sri Lanka as 'India's island region'. Using the chapter, explain why that is not right.
questions.a: (a) India is the seventh-largest country in the world. (b) The Himalayas. (c) The great mountain zone, the plains of the Ganga and the Indus, the desert region, the southern peninsula and the islands. (d) Sri Lanka is a neighbouring country that forms the Indian Subcontinent with India; it is not part of India, so it is not one of India's regions. India's islands region means its own islands, such as Lakshadweep and the Andaman and Nicobar Islands.
s: (a) States that India is the seventh-largest country
(b) Names the Himalayas
(c) Names all five regions
(d) Explains Sri Lanka is a neighbouring country of the subcontinent, not an Indian region; India's islands are its own island groups

questions.q:
A student argues: 'India's natural boundaries cut it off from the rest of Asia, so all of India inside those boundaries must have much the same land and climate.' Evaluate this argument.
(a) State what the chapter says the natural boundaries do.
(b) Contrast the climate of Ladakh with that of the Thar Desert, using the chapter's facts.
(c) Contrast the landform of the Gangetic Plains with that of the Peninsular Plateau.
(d) Give one more example of a region with very different conditions.
(e) Give your verdict, using the chapter's summary about the variety of conditions.
questions.a: (a) The boundaries separate India from the rest of the continent and have shaped its climate, culture and history. (b) Ladakh is a cold desert with winter temperatures below -30 degrees C and very little rain; the Thar has very high daytime temperatures, cold nights and little water. (c) The Gangetic Plains are flat, fertile land fed by Himalayan rivers; the Peninsular Plateau is a very old, raised, triangular landform bordered by the Ghats. (d) For example, the Meghalaya hills get one of the highest rainfalls in the world, or the Himadri is snow-covered all year. (e) The argument is wrong: being separated from Asia does not make India uniform. The chapter says India's diverse features have created a variety of conditions of soil, flora, fauna, life and economic opportunities.
s: (a) States that the boundaries separate India from the rest of Asia and shaped its climate, culture and history
(b) Contrasts Ladakh (below -30 degrees C, little rain) with the Thar (very hot days, cold nights)
(c) Contrasts the flat, fertile plains with the old, raised plateau
(d) Gives one more contrasting region with a chapter fact
(e) Verdict: the argument fails, because the chapter says the features create a variety of conditions

questions.q: Which range of the Himalayas stays snow-covered throughout the year and is home to Mount Everest and Kanchenjunga?
questions.a: The Himadri, or Greater Himalayas.

questions.q: A biology class wants a Himalayan study camp in a range with a moderate climate, rich biodiversity and towns nearby where people live, but NOT in the outermost foothills. Which range fits all of these needs?
o: The Gangetic Plains below the hills
questions.a: The Himachal (Lower Himalayas): moderate climate, rich biodiversity and human habitation, and it is not the outermost range.

questions.q:
Match each item in Column A with what the chapter says about it in Column B.
Column A: 1. Gaumukh  2. Kath-kuni  3. Rhododendron  4. Eight Thousanders
Column B: a. a flower from which a type of sherbet is made  b. Himalayan peaks over 8000 metres high  c. the place where the Bhagirathi River originates  d. a house style of local stone and wood
questions.a: 1-c, 2-d, 3-a, 4-b: Gaumukh is where the Bhagirathi originates, kath-kuni is a stone-and-wood house style, a sherbet is made from rhododendron, and the Eight Thousanders are peaks over 8000 m.

questions.q:
Assertion (A): Life in the Himadri is tough, and there are not many human settlements there.
Reason (R): Hill stations such as Shimla and Nainital are located in the Himachal.
Choose the correct option.
o: Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
A is true, but R is false.
A is false, but R is true.
questions.a: Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A. Settlements are few in the Himadri because it is the highest, most rugged and snow-covered range; where the hill stations are does not explain that.

questions.q: True or False? 'The Himachal is the range that serves as a transition zone between the Himalayas and the Gangetic Plains.' Give the verdict and the corrected statement.
questions.a: False. It is the Shivalik Hills (the Outer Himalayas), the outermost and lowest range of rolling hills and dense forests, that serve as the transition zone between the Himalayas and the Gangetic Plains. The Himachal lies further north, south of the Himadri.
s: States the verdict: False
Corrects it: the Shivalik Hills, the outermost and lowest range, are the transition zone

questions.q: (a) What does the word 'Himalaya' mean, and from which two Sanskrit words is it made? (b) What does the name 'Gaumukh' mean?
questions.a: (a) 'Abode of snow': it combines hima, meaning 'snow', and alaya, meaning 'abode' or 'dwelling'. (b) 'Cow's Mouth'.
s: (a) Gives 'abode of snow' from hima (snow) and alaya (abode)
(b) States that Gaumukh means 'Cow's Mouth'

questions.q: The Himalayas are broadly divided into three main ranges. Name each range and give one feature of each.
questions.a: The Himadri (Greater Himalayas): the highest and most rugged, snow-covered all year, few settlements. The Himachal (Lower Himalayas): south of the Himadri, moderate climate, hill stations such as Shimla. The Shivalik Hills (Outer Himalayas): the outermost and lowest range of rolling hills and dense forests, rich in wildlife.
s: Himadri named with one correct feature
Himachal named with one correct feature
Shivalik Hills named with one correct feature

questions.q: Rahul says, 'People go to the Himalayas only to climb the Eight Thousanders or to trek.' Show that he is wrong by giving three other reasons, from the chapter, why people go to the Himalayas: (a) a reason linked to belief at the mountains themselves; (b) a reason linked to the Gangotri Glacier; (c) a reason linked to the Himachal range, with your final verdict on Rahul's claim.
questions.a: (a) The mountains themselves are considered sacred; temples and monasteries have been built in them, and monks and spiritual seekers come from around the world to pray and meditate. (b) The Gangotri Glacier is considered sacred and attracts many pilgrims. (c) The Himachal has a moderate climate and popular hill stations such as Nainital, Darjeeling, Shimla and Mussoorie. Verdict: Rahul is wrong; people also go to the Himalayas to pray and meditate, as pilgrims, and to visit hill stations.
s: (a) Sacred mountains with temples and monasteries, where monks and spiritual seekers come to pray and meditate
(b) The Gangotri Glacier is sacred and attracts pilgrims
(c) Names a hill station of the Himachal (moderate climate) and gives the verdict that Rahul is wrong

questions.q: A school club in Haridwar can make one Himalayan study trip this year. Trip 1 goes to Gaumukh in Uttarakhand; Trip 2 goes to the Great Himalayan National Park in Himachal Pradesh. The club's theme is 'How the Himalayas give water to the plains'. (a) Which trip fits the theme better, and why? (b) Gaumukh lies at the edge of which glacier, and how large is that glacier compared with others in the Indian Himalayas? (c) Why does this glacier attract many pilgrims? (d) Name a different theme for which Trip 2 would be the better choice, with one reason.
questions.a: (a) Trip 1, to Gaumukh, because the Bhagirathi River, a major tributary of the Ganga, begins there. (b) The Gangotri Glacier; it is one of the largest glaciers in the Indian Himalayas. (c) It is considered sacred. (d) A theme on wildlife or biodiversity: the Great Himalayan National Park has a wide diversity of plants and animals.
s: (a) Chooses Trip 1, linking Gaumukh to the start of the Bhagirathi and the Ganga
(b) Names the Gangotri Glacier as one of the largest in the Indian Himalayas
(c) States that the glacier is considered sacred
(d) Gives a biodiversity or wildlife theme for Trip 2 with a chapter reason

questions.q:
Tell the story of how the Himalayas were formed, and why they are still changing, by answering each part.
(a) Of which bigger landmass was India once a part?
(b) In which direction did India move after it broke away, and with which landmass did it collide?
(c) About how many years ago did this collision happen?
(d) Explain, using the chapter's carpet example, how the collision formed the Himalayas.
(e) Explain why the Himalayas are still growing taller today, and say about how much they rise each year.
questions.a: (a) Gondwana. (b) North; it collided with Eurasia. (c) About 50 million years ago. (d) As India pushed against Eurasia, the land between them crumpled and rose up, just as a carpet wrinkles when you push it; that crumpled, raised land is the Himalayas. (e) India is still pushing into Asia, very slowly (about five centimetres a year), so the land keeps being pushed up; the Himalayas rise about five millimetres each year.
s: (a) Gondwana
(b) North, colliding with Eurasia
(c) About 50 million years ago
(d) Explains that the pushed land crumpled and rose up, like a carpet wrinkling when pushed
(e) Explains that India is still pushing into Asia, so the Himalayas rise about 5 mm a year

questions.q: Why is the landscape of Ladakh called 'moonland'?
o: Its terrain resembles that of the moon
It can be seen only on moonlit nights
It is coldest when the moon is full
Its main lake is named after the moon
questions.a: Because its terrain resembles that of the moon.

questions.q: In the name 'Pangong Tso', what does the word 'tso' mean?
questions.a: 'Tso' means lake.

questions.q: A student pairs some features of Ladakh with their causes. Which pairing matches the chapter?
o: Eroded mountain shapes - wind and rain wearing down the mountains
Salty water of Pangong Tso - sea water left behind by an ocean
Very cold winters - the hot sands of a nearby desert
The name 'moonland' - the region's heavy rainfall
questions.a: Wind and rain have eroded the mountains into the shapes seen in Ladakh. (Pangong Tso's salt comes from minerals dissolved from the surrounding mountains, not from sea water.)

questions.q:
Read the statements about Ladakh and the Gangetic Plains.
I. Winter temperatures in Ladakh drop below -30 degrees C.
II. The Gangetic Plains are nourished by rivers that originate in the Western Ghats.
III. A large proportion of India's population lives in the Gangetic Plains.
Which of these statements is/are correct?
questions.a: Statements I and III are correct. Statement II is wrong: the rivers that nourish the Gangetic Plains originate in the Himalayas.

questions.q: (a) Name two wild animals that live in Ladakh despite its harsh conditions. (b) Name one festival for which Ladakh is known.
questions.a: (a) Any two of the snow leopard, the ibex and the Tibetan antelope. (b) Losar or the Hemis Festival.
s: (a) Names two of snow leopard, ibex, Tibetan antelope
(b) Names Losar or the Hemis Festival

questions.q: (a) The word 'desert' usually brings to mind a hot place. What feature of Ladakh makes it a desert even though it is cold? (b) Using your answer to (a), what can you infer about farming in Ladakh compared with farming on the Gangetic Plains?
questions.a: (a) Ladakh gets very little rainfall, so it is a (cold) desert. (b) Inference: with very little rain and rugged, rocky terrain, Ladakh has little water and little flat, fertile land, so farming there is likely to be far more limited than on the plains, which get water and minerals from the Himalayan rivers.
s: (a) States that Ladakh gets very little rainfall
(b) Infers that farming in Ladakh is more limited than on the river-fed plains, linking it to little water and rocky land

questions.q: Give three ways in which the rivers and the flat land of the Gangetic Plains help the people who live there.
questions.a: Any three: the rivers bring water and minerals that make the soil fertile, ideal for farming; the rivers are a source for generating electricity; the flat land has allowed a large road and railway network to move people and goods over long distances; the rivers have been used for travel and trade for millennia.
s: First correct way (fertile soil for farming from river water and minerals)
Second correct way (electricity, or travel and trade on the rivers)
Third correct way (flat land allows roads and railways)

questions.q: Neha says, 'The rocks of Ladakh are made of sand and clay because wind blew the sand there, and the wind also shaped the mountains.' Is she right, wrong or partly right? Explain using the chapter.
questions.a: Partly right. The chapter says wind and rain eroded the mountains into the shapes we see, so the second part is right. But the rocks are made largely of sand and clay because the folded portion was once part of an ocean when India collided with Eurasia, not because wind blew sand there.
s: Verdict: partly right
Agrees that wind (with rain) eroded the mountains into their shapes
Corrects the cause of sand and clay: the folded land was once part of an ocean

questions.q:
Sunita farms on the Gangetic Plains in Bihar and can lease one of two plots for the same rent. Plot P has 2.5 hectares beside a tributary of the Ganga; the river gives water all year, so she can grow two crops a year on the same field, and each crop gives about 3 tonnes of grain per hectare. Plot Q has 4 hectares, 8 km from any river, watered only by rain; it gives one crop a year of about 2 tonnes per hectare.
(a) Name the three river systems the chapter says nourish the plains, and the mountains they come from.
(b) Using the chapter, explain why the soil of Plot P is likely to be richer than the soil of Plot Q.
(c) How many tonnes of grain can each plot give in a year?
(d) Which plot should Sunita lease? Decide by weighing Plot Q's larger area against your answer to (c).
questions.a: (a) The Ganga, Indus and Brahmaputra river systems, which come from the Himalayas. (b) The rivers bring minerals that enrich the soil, so land beside a river, like Plot P, gets both water and minerals, while Plot Q, far from any river, depends on rain alone. (c) Plot P: 2.5 x 2 x 3 = 15 tonnes; Plot Q: 4 x 1 x 2 = 8 tonnes. (d) Plot P: although Plot Q is 1.5 hectares larger, Plot P gives 15 tonnes against 8 tonnes, nearly twice as much, because river water allows two crops a year on mineral-rich soil.
s: (a) Names the Ganga, Indus and Brahmaputra and says they come from the Himalayas
(b) Explains that the rivers bring water and minerals that enrich the soil, which Plot Q lacks
(c) Calculates 15 tonnes for P and 8 tonnes for Q
(d) Chooses Plot P, weighing Q's larger area against P's greater yearly harvest

questions.q:
A group of 24 students will spend 4 days studying Pangong Tso and the landscape around it, and must visit the lake every day. Site A is a camp beside the lake; fresh water there must be carried from a stream 7 km away by the group's two yaks, which can make 2 water trips a day in total, carrying 48 litres per trip. Site B is a camp beside the stream, 9 km from the lake, so each day's lake visit means an 18 km round trip. Each student needs 3 litres of drinking water a day.
(a) Why can the group not drink the water of Pangong Tso?
(b) Why can the group not plan to collect rainwater instead?
(c) How many yak trips are needed at Site A for the whole camp, and can the yaks manage them in 4 days?
(d) Which site should the group choose? Weigh the carried water at Site A against the daily walk from Site B.
questions.a: (a) Pangong Tso has salty water, unlike most other lakes, because minerals dissolve into it from the surrounding mountain areas. (b) Ladakh is a cold desert with very little rainfall. (c) 24 x 3 x 4 = 288 litres; 288 / 48 = 6 trips. The yaks can make 2 x 4 = 8 trips in 4 days, so 6 trips are within their limit. (d) Either site earns the mark if the choice is weighed with the data. For example, Site A: the data shows its water problem can be solved with 6 of the 8 possible yak trips, while Site B would add an 18 km round trip every day across rugged, rocky terrain to reach the lake the group must study. Site B's only gain, fresh water on the spot, does not outweigh this. A student may instead choose Site B, arguing that fresh water on the spot is safer than relying on two yaks for 6 of only 8 possible trips, which leaves little margin, and accepting the 18 km daily walk.
s: (a) States that the lake water is salty because of minerals dissolved from the surrounding mountains
(b) States that Ladakh gets very little rainfall
(c) Calculates 288 litres and 6 trips, and compares with the 8 trips the yaks can make
(d) Chooses either site and weighs it with the data: Site A's 6 of 8 yak trips against Site B's 18 km daily round trip

questions.q: Which city, located in the middle of the Thar Desert, is called the 'Golden City'?
questions.a: Jaisalmer, whose fort is a UNESCO World Heritage site.

questions.q: A museum label about the Zawar mines in the Aravallis must be accurate to the chapter. Which label should it use?
o: Here, over eight centuries ago, Indians first mastered zinc extraction
Zinc was first mined here 2.5 billion years ago, as the hills formed
These mines in the Thar Desert first produced copper for the world
Zinc extraction began here only in the last hundred years or so
questions.a: Evidence from the ancient Zawar mines shows that over eight centuries ago Indians were the first in the world to master the extraction of zinc.

questions.q:
Match each item in Column A with its description in Column B.
Column A: 1. The Aravalli Hills  2. Taanka  3. Sand dunes  4. Pushkar Mela
Column B: a. hill-like formations shaped by the wind, sometimes as high as 150 metres  b. a system that stores rainwater, often for drinking  c. among the oldest mountains in the world  d. a fair at the edge of the Thar Desert where camel vendors gather
questions.a: 1-c, 2-b, 3-a, 4-d: the Aravallis are among the oldest mountains in the world, a taanka stores rainwater, sand dunes are wind-shaped hill-like formations up to 150 m high, and the Pushkar Mela at the edge of the Thar is where camel vendors gather.

questions.q:
Assertion (A): The Thar Desert acts as a natural barrier that deters human and animal movement.
Reason (R): The Thar has mild temperatures through both the day and the night.
Choose the correct option.
o: A is true, but R is false.
Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is false, but R is true.
questions.a: A is true, but R is false. The Thar has very high daytime temperatures and cold nights, and a lack of water; these harsh conditions are what make it a barrier.

questions.q: True or False? 'Mount Abu, the highest peak of the Aravallis, rises over 1700 m, but most of the Aravalli hills are much lower.' Give the verdict and the reason.
questions.a: True. Mount Abu towers at over 1700 m, while most of the Aravalli hills are between 300 and 900 metres high.
s: States the verdict: True
Gives the chapter's figures: Mount Abu over 1700 m, most hills 300 to 900 m

questions.q: (a) Name any two minerals in which the Aravallis are rich. (b) Which two kinds of activity have these minerals supported for centuries?
questions.a: (a) Any two of marble, granite, zinc and copper. (b) Mining and construction.
s: (a) Names two of marble, granite, zinc, copper
(b) Names mining and construction

questions.q: Give three harsh conditions of the Thar Desert that the chapter mentions, and say what effect these conditions have on movement across the desert.
questions.a: Very high daytime temperatures, cold nights and a lack of access to water (the land is a vast arid region of sand dunes). Because of these conditions the desert acts as a natural barrier that deters human and animal movement.
s: Names two harsh conditions (very hot days, cold nights)
Names a third condition (lack of water / arid land)
States that these make the Thar a natural barrier deterring human and animal movement

questions.q: A history teacher asks why so many forts were built in the Aravalli Hills. (a) Name three historic forts that the chapter says are located in the Aravallis. (b) What did Kumbhalgarh Fort's location in the hills do for its defenders? (c) Using (b), explain why hill ranges suited fort builders.
questions.a: (a) Chittorgarh, Kumbhalgarh and Ranthambore. (b) Its location in the hills proved to be an excellent deterrent to the enemy. (c) Hills are hard to reach and climb, so a fort among them is difficult for an enemy to attack, which made the Aravallis a good place for forts.
s: (a) Names Chittorgarh, Kumbhalgarh and Ranthambore
(b) States that the hill location deterred the enemy
(c) Explains that hills make a fort hard for an enemy to approach and attack

questions.q:
A company asks permission to quarry marble from an Aravalli ridge that lies just east of the Thar Desert, near a group of villages. The ridge is 12 km long, and the company plans to cut away 3 km of it over ten years. It promises 400 jobs. Villagers fear that the desert will reach their fields.
(a) Name any two of the places that the chapter says the Aravalli range spans.
(b) What important role does the chapter say the Aravallis play for the land to their east?
(c) What percentage of the ridge's length would be cut away?
(d) Should the permission be given? Give a decision that weighs the jobs against the villagers' fear, using (b) and (c).
questions.a: (a) Any two of Delhi, Rajasthan, Haryana and Gujarat. (b) They act as a natural barrier, preventing the Thar Desert from expanding further eastward. (c) 3 / 12 = 25 per cent. (d) A reasoned decision: for example, refuse or limit it, because removing a quarter of the ridge would open a gap in the barrier that holds the desert back from the villages' fields; or allow a smaller cut with conditions, because mining has supported people for centuries and 400 jobs matter. The answer must weigh both sides.
s: (a) Names two of Delhi, Rajasthan, Haryana, Gujarat
(b) States that the Aravallis stop the Thar spreading east
(c) Calculates 25 per cent
(d) Makes a decision that weighs the jobs against the barrier role, using (b) and (c)

questions.q: The Thar Desert and the Aravalli Hills lie side by side in north-western India, yet a drive between them feels like entering a different geography. Compare the two under these heads: (a) what the land looks like and how it was shaped; (b) height; (c) age, or how long the feature has existed, where the chapter says; (d) resources, or what people get from it; (e) the role each plays as a barrier, and one way this links the two.
questions.a: (a) The Thar is a vast arid stretch of sand dunes shaped by the wind; the Aravallis are a range with many peaks and ridges. (b) Thar dunes rise as high as 150 metres; most Aravalli hills are 300 to 900 m and Mount Abu is over 1700 m. (c) The Aravallis are among the oldest mountains in the world, about 2.5 billion years old; the chapter gives no age for the Thar. (d) The Aravallis are rich in marble, granite, zinc and copper and have historic forts; Thar people depend on scarce water, stored in taanka or kunds. (e) The Thar is a barrier because its harsh conditions deter movement; the Aravallis are a barrier that stops the Thar from spreading east. The link: the Aravallis hold back the very desert that lies beside them.
s: (a) Contrasts wind-shaped sand dunes with a range of many peaks and ridges
(b) Compares heights: dunes up to 150 m, hills 300 to 900 m, Mount Abu over 1700 m
(c) Gives the Aravallis' age of about 2.5 billion years
(d) Contrasts the Aravallis' minerals with the Thar's water scarcity and storage
(e) Compares their barrier roles and states the link that the Aravallis hold back the Thar

questions.q: By what other name is the northern portion of the Western Ghats known?
questions.a: The Sahyadri Hills.

questions.q: Jog Falls in Karnataka drops over the edge of a plateau. How does the chapter say the power of such a waterfall is put to use?
o: It is turned into electricity by special turbines
It is used to build a delta at the river's mouth
It carries sand that forms dunes near the coast
It washes minerals that make lakes salty
questions.a: The power of the waterfall is converted into electricity (hydroelectricity) through special turbines.

questions.q:
Read the statements about the Peninsular Plateau.
I. The Eastern Ghats are taller than the Western Ghats.
II. The Narmada and the Tapti drain into the Arabian Sea.
III. The Deccan Plateau lies to the west of the Western Ghats.
Which of these statements is/are correct?
questions.a: Only statement II is correct. The Western Ghats are the taller range, and the Deccan Plateau lies between the Western and Eastern Ghats.

questions.q:
Assertion (A): All the major rivers of the Peninsular Plateau flow into the Bay of Bengal.
Reason (R): The Peninsular Plateau tilts a little to the east.
Choose the correct option.
o: A is false, but R is true.
Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true, but R is false.
questions.a: A is false, but R is true. The plateau does tilt a little to the east, so rivers such as the Godavari, Krishna and Mahanadi flow east, but the Narmada and Tapti flow west into the Arabian Sea.

questions.q: (a) What is a plateau? (b) What is a peninsula?
questions.a: (a) A plateau is a landform that rises up from the surrounding land and has a more or less flat surface; some of its sides are often steep slopes. (b) A peninsula is a piece of land surrounded by water on three sides.
s: (a) Defines a plateau as raised land with a more or less flat top
(b) Defines a peninsula as land surrounded by water on three sides

questions.q: A nature club on a hill walk in Kerala finds a plant whose leaves have sticky traps with small insects stuck to them. On the same walk they see a lion-tailed macaque. (a) Using the chapter, identify what kind of plant this is and explain how it gets food. (b) In which mountain range shown in the chapter were these two found, and what quality of that range, given in the chapter, do they show?
questions.a: (a) An insectivorous plant: it feeds on insects, catching small insects in sticky traps and digesting them. (b) The Western Ghats; they show the range's rich biodiversity.
s: (a) Identifies an insectivorous plant that catches insects in sticky traps and digests them
(b) Names the Western Ghats and links the finds to its rich biodiversity

questions.q: (a) Name three tribal communities that live in the dense forests of the plateau. (b) Name two states over which tribal communities are largely spread. (c) What does the chapter say their ways of life are closely connected to?
questions.a: (a) Any three of the Santhal, Gond, Baiga, Bhil and Korku. (b) Any two of Jharkhand, West Bengal, Odisha, Assam, Madhya Pradesh, Chhattisgarh, Maharashtra, Telangana and Gujarat. (c) Nature; they have distinct languages, traditions and ways of life closely connected to Nature.
s: (a) Names three of Santhal, Gond, Baiga, Bhil, Korku
(b) Names two correct states
(c) States that their ways of life are closely connected to Nature

questions.q: Dev says, 'The Deccan is a vast area of flat highland, so it cannot be part of a plateau, because a plateau must have steep sides everywhere.' Is he right? Explain using the chapter's meaning of a plateau and what borders the Deccan.
questions.a: No. The chapter says a plateau rises from the surrounding land and has a more or less flat surface, and only some of its sides are often steep; it does not need steep sides everywhere. The Deccan's flat highland is exactly that flat top, and it lies between the Western Ghats, which are tall with steep sides, and the lower Eastern Ghats, all part of the Peninsular Plateau.
s: Verdict: No
Uses the chapter's meaning: raised land with a more or less flat surface, only some sides steep
Places the Deccan between the Western and Eastern Ghats as part of the Peninsular Plateau

questions.q: A student's project says, 'The Western Ghats, the Eastern Ghats and the Deccan Plateau are three separate landforms with nothing in common.' Evaluate this claim. (a) Describe the shape and age of the Peninsular Plateau. (b) Explain how the Western and Eastern Ghats differ and what they do for the plateau. (c) Say where the Deccan Plateau lies. (d) Give one thing that links all three, and your verdict.
questions.a: (a) The Peninsular Plateau is a triangular, very old land formation in the middle and south of India, surrounded by water on three sides. (b) The Western Ghats are taller and run along the western coast like a wall; the Eastern Ghats are lower and broken into smaller hills along the eastern coast. Both border the plateau. (c) The Deccan Plateau, a vast area of flat highlands, lies between the two Ghats. (d) All three are parts of the same Peninsular Plateau; for example, rivers like the Godavari, Krishna and Kaveri flow across the plateau from west to east. Verdict: the claim is wrong; they are parts of one landform.
s: (a) Describes the plateau as triangular and very old
(b) Contrasts the tall Western Ghats with the lower, broken Eastern Ghats as its borders
(c) Places the Deccan between the two Ghats
(d) Gives a link (one plateau, rivers crossing it) and the verdict that the claim is wrong

questions.q: 'The Peninsular Plateau gives India water, power, minerals, a home for many communities and sights that draw visitors.' Justify this statement with five points from the chapter: (a) water; (b) power from water; (c) minerals and fuel; (d) forests and the people who live in them; (e) sights that draw visitors, with one honour given to part of the plateau.
questions.a: (a) Rivers such as the Godavari, Krishna and Kaveri flow across the plateau and provide water for farming to millions of people. (b) Waterfalls form where rivers flow over the uneven, rocky surface; they help in hydroelectric power generation and give water for irrigation. (c) The plateau is rich in minerals, and its coal is an important resource, especially for producing electricity. (d) Dense forests on the plateau are home to tribal communities such as the Santhal, Gond, Baiga, Bhil and Korku. (e) Its many beautiful waterfalls attract tourists, including those flowing down the steep sides of the Western Ghats in the monsoon; the Western Ghats have been declared a UNESCO World Heritage Site.
s: (a) Rivers giving water for farming to millions
(b) Waterfalls used for hydroelectric power and irrigation
(c) Minerals and coal for electricity
(d) Forests that are home to tribal communities, with examples
(e) Waterfalls that attract tourists, and the Western Ghats as a UNESCO World Heritage Site

questions.q: Which city on the west coast does the chapter call India's financial centre?
questions.a: Mumbai.

questions.q: The chapter calls the Andaman and Nicobar Islands 'outposts of India'. What does it mean by this?
o: Their location lets India keep an eye on the ocean
They are the oldest land formation in India
They are made of coral, like Lakshadweep
They lie in the Arabian Sea, close to Kerala
questions.a: Their location is very important: like outposts, they let India keep an eye on the ocean.

questions.q:
Match each place in Column A with its feature in Column B.
Column A: 1. Lakshadweep  2. Andaman and Nicobar Islands  3. Sundarbans  4. Meghalaya Plateau
Column B: a. one of the highest rainfalls in the world  b. 36 islands made of coral  c. home of the Royal Bengal Tiger  d. more than 500 volcanic islands
questions.a: 1-b, 2-d, 3-c, 4-a: Lakshadweep has 36 coral islands, the Andaman and Nicobar group has more than 500 volcanic islands, the Sundarbans are home to the Royal Bengal Tiger, and the Meghalaya Plateau gets one of the highest rainfalls in the world.

questions.q: True or False? 'Most rivers of India's west coast rise in the Eastern Ghats, flow slowly and build wide deltas.' Give the verdict and the corrected statement.
questions.a: False. Most rivers of the west coast originate in the Western Ghats, flow swiftly and form estuaries, the largest being those of the Narmada and the Tapti.
s: States the verdict: False
Corrects it: they rise in the Western Ghats, flow swiftly and form estuaries

questions.q: (a) The west coast of India stretches from Gujarat to Kerala. Name the three states it passes through in between. (b) Besides estuaries, name the two other features that the chapter says shape this coastline.
questions.a: (a) Maharashtra, Goa and Karnataka. (b) Coves and creeks.
s: (a) Names Maharashtra, Goa and Karnataka
(b) Names coves and creeks

questions.q: A student mixes up India's two island groups. Distinguish Lakshadweep from the Andaman and Nicobar Islands under three heads: (a) the sea each lies in, and the mainland coast Lakshadweep is close to; (b) how each archipelago is divided; (c) which group has India's only active volcano, and its name.
questions.a: (a) Lakshadweep lies in the Arabian Sea, close to the Malabar coast of Kerala; the Andaman and Nicobar Islands lie in the Bay of Bengal. (b) Lakshadweep is a single archipelago of islands, not all of them inhabited; the Andaman and Nicobar archipelago is divided into two distinct groups, the Andaman Islands and the Nicobar Islands. (c) The Andaman and Nicobar Islands: Barren Island is the only active volcano in India.
s: (a) Arabian Sea near the Malabar coast of Kerala versus the Bay of Bengal
(b) One archipelago versus two distinct groups, Andaman and Nicobar
(c) Names Barren Island in the Andaman and Nicobar Islands

questions.q:
A Class 7 group from Kolkata is preparing for a boat trip into the Sundarbans. Their guide writes: 'We will travel through mangrove forests where two great rivers and their tributaries meet the sea. River, sea and land combine here in a way found almost nowhere else. The area is shared between two countries.' Suppose the whole delta covers about 10,000 square km.
(a) Name the two great rivers in whose delta the Sundarbans lie.
(b) How is a delta formed?
(c) About how many square km of this delta lie in India?
(d) Name the famous animal the group hopes to see, and the status the Sundarbans have from UNESCO.
questions.a: (a) The Ganga and the Brahmaputra. (b) A delta forms at the mouth of a river when it deposits sediments into a larger body of water; over time the sediments build up into a triangular or fan-shaped area. (c) About half of the delta is in India, so about 5,000 square km. (d) The Royal Bengal Tiger; the Sundarbans are a UNESCO Heritage site.
s: (a) Names the Ganga and the Brahmaputra
(b) Explains that a river deposits sediments at its mouth, building a triangular or fan-shaped area
(c) Uses 'about half in India' to get about 5,000 square km
(d) Names the Royal Bengal Tiger and the UNESCO Heritage status

questions.q:
The Rao family wants to grow as much rice as possible, and also to sell part of its harvest through a port. It is offered two plots at the same price. Plot A has 4 hectares of flat land in the Krishna delta on the east coast. Plot B is on the west coast, close to a busy port city, where the hills of the Western Ghats come very close to the Arabian Sea; only 1.5 hectares of it is flat, and the rest is slope.
(a) Why does the east coast have wide plains and fertile deltas?
(b) The chapter notes that on the west coast the hills of the Western Ghats come very close to the Arabian Sea. What can you infer about the flat land there?
(c) How many times as much flat land does Plot A have as Plot B? Round to one decimal place.
(d) Name the advantage the chapter gives the west coast. Then decide which plot the Raos should buy, weighing that advantage against your answers to (a) to (c).
questions.a: (a) The east coast lies between the Eastern Ghats and the Bay of Bengal; rivers such as the Mahanadi, Godavari, Krishna and Kaveri deposit sediments at their mouths and build fertile deltas, making the land ideal for farming. (b) Inference: with the hills so close to the sea, there can be only a narrow strip of flat land between them. (c) 4 / 1.5 = 2.67, about 2.7 times. (d) The west coast has many important ports and cities that have been centres of economic activity for millennia, so Plot B is close to trade. But the Raos' first aim is the largest rice crop, and Plot A gives about 2.7 times the flat land, on fertile delta soil; so Plot A is the better buy, and its rice can still be sent to a port by road or rail. (Plot B earns the mark only if the answer weighs its 2.7 times smaller flat area against the port.)
s: (a) Explains that east-coast rivers build fertile deltas, giving wide plains ideal for farming
(b) Infers that only a narrow strip of flat land lies between the hills and the sea
(c) Calculates about 2.7 times
(d) Names the west coast's ports and cities and makes a decision weighing them against the larger, fertile delta plot

questions.q: A newspaper asks readers why the Andaman Islands are worth learning about, even though they lie far from the mainland. Write an answer under four heads: (a) who were jailed there, where, and under what conditions; (b) why that prison complex has been preserved; (c) what the islands offer for nature; (d) who made India's islands their home first, and how long ago.
questions.a: (a) Many of India's freedom fighters were jailed there under the most severe conditions, in a prison complex called the Cellular Jail. (b) It has been preserved to remind us of the tremendous sacrifices our forefathers made so that we could be free. (c) They are home to a variety of plants and animals, with coral reefs and beautiful beaches. (d) Several ancient tribes made these islands their home tens of thousands of years ago.
s: (a) Freedom fighters jailed in the Cellular Jail under the most severe conditions
(b) Preserved to remind us of the sacrifices made for our freedom
(c) Variety of flora and fauna, coral reefs or beaches
(d) Ancient tribes, tens of thousands of years ago

questions.q:
A film crew based in Chennai has exactly 6 days to film two scenes for a programme: Scene 1, 'water cut off from the sea by a natural barrier', and Scene 2, 'land built up by a river at its mouth'. It can choose from Pulicat Lake, the Kaveri delta, the Godavari delta and the Narmada estuary. Filming takes 1 day at each stop, and the crew must start and end in Chennai. Travel days in its plan: Chennai to Pulicat Lake 1, Chennai to the Kaveri delta 1, Chennai to the Godavari delta 2, Pulicat Lake to the Kaveri delta 2, Pulicat Lake to the Godavari delta 2, Chennai to the Narmada estuary 3.
(a) Which site fits Scene 1? Give the chapter's meaning of the landform it shows.
(b) Which sites fit Scene 2? Explain how this landform is built.
(c) Why can the Narmada estuary not be used for Scene 2, even though the Narmada is a major river?
(d) Work out the total days (travel plus filming) for the plan Chennai - Pulicat Lake - Kaveri delta - Chennai and for the plan Chennai - Pulicat Lake - Godavari delta - Chennai.
(e) Which plan should the crew choose? Justify it using (a) to (d).
questions.a: (a) Pulicat Lake: it is a lagoon, a body of water separated from larger bodies of water by a natural barrier. (b) The Kaveri delta and the Godavari delta: a delta forms at the mouth of a river when it deposits sediments into a larger body of water; over time the sediments build up into a triangular or fan-shaped area. (c) The Narmada flows west into the Arabian Sea, and like most west-coast rivers it forms an estuary at its mouth, not a delta, so it does not show land built up at the mouth. (d) Kaveri plan: travel 1 + 2 + 1 = 4 days, filming 2 days, total 6 days. Godavari plan: travel 1 + 2 + 2 = 5 days, filming 2 days, total 7 days. (e) The Kaveri plan: it is the only plan that films a lagoon for Scene 1 and a delta for Scene 2 within the 6 days; the Godavari plan also shows the right landforms but needs 7 days, and the Narmada estuary does not show a delta at all.
s: (a) Names Pulicat Lake as a lagoon, with the chapter's meaning
(b) Names the Kaveri and Godavari deltas and explains that sediments deposited at the mouth build up a fan-shaped area
(c) Explains that the west-flowing Narmada forms an estuary, not a delta
(d) Calculates 6 days for the Kaveri plan and 7 days for the Godavari plan
(e) Chooses the Kaveri plan as the only one that fits both scenes in 6 days, using (a) to (d)
